title: Agent Evals: Finally, With The Map

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk is fundamentally about evaluation design, presenting a structured map of agent evaluation metrics and methodology. The framework applies broadly to any AI agent system rather than targeting a specific vertical. The content covers both offline evaluation during development and online testing in production, plus Eval Ops as an ongoing operational concern. Requires familiarity with AI agents, RAG pipelines, and LLMOps, but is primarily a conceptual overview rather than deep technical implementation. The presentation introduces a principled taxonomy and framework for organizing agent evaluation rather than a specific tool or system. Multiple evidence anchors directly support the classification across all key claims.

summary: The presentation by Ari Heluk from Root Signals provides a structured map of AI agent evaluation, arguing it should move beyond ad hoc metric lists toward a principled, comprehensive framework. The map divides evaluation into two core dimensions: semantic and behavioral. Semantic evaluation addresses how the agent's representations of reality relate to actual reality, split into single-turn aspects (coherence, consistency, safety, alignment with organizational values, policy adherence, RAG-specific metrics like context recall, faithfulness, answer-question relevance, and factfulness) and multi-turn aspects (chat conversation consistency, topic adherence, and reasoning trace evaluation). Behavioral evaluation addresses how actions and tools contribute to goal achievement, also split into single-step aspects (instruction following, tool characteristic extraction, tool selection, output quality, error handling, format correctness) and multi-turn aspects (action convergence toward goals, plan consistency and quality). A key symmetry is highlighted: representations are grounded via truthfulness (often through RAG and tracing), while behaviors are grounded via goal achievement and utility. The ultimate metric is goal achievement; all other measures along the way are proxy metrics. Practical considerations include cost and latency optimization, step count minimization, tracing and debugging, error management (distinguishing tool usage errors from semantic inference errors), and the critical distinction between offline (development) and online (production) testing. Tool-specific metrics can leverage traditional software testing for API-like tools. The presentation introduces 'Eval Ops' as a special case of LLMOps: when using LLM-as-judge techniques, a single-tier approach optimizes only the agent, but a double-tier approach recognizes the judge/evaluation flow itself requires optimization for cost, latency, and uncertainty. Eval Ops operates on different entities than general LLMOps and demands different thinking, software implementations, and resourcing.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Agent evaluation is divided into semantic (representation-reality relationship) and behavioral (action-goal achievement) dimensions, each with single-turn and multi-turn sub-dimensions.
Semantic single-turn evaluation includes universal virtues (consistency, safety), value alignment, policy adherence, and RAG-specific metrics (context recall, faithfulness, relevance, factfulness).
Multi-turn semantic evaluation covers conversation consistency, topic adherence, and increasingly, reasoning trace / Chain of Thought evaluation.
Behavioral evaluation covers tool selection, output quality, error handling, and format correctness at the single-step level, and plan consistency and goal convergence at the multi-step level.
Truthfulness grounds representations (via RAG/tracing); goal achievement and utility ground behaviors — the latter is the ultimate metric, with all else being proxy metrics.
Cost, latency, step count optimization, tracing, debugging, and the offline-vs-online testing distinction are essential practical considerations outside the core map.

Eval Ops is introduced as a special case of LLMOps: a double-tier approach that optimizes both the agent's operative LLM flow and the LLM-judge evaluation flow, recognizing evaluations as complex, expensive, and slow enough to warrant their own category.
Understand the structured division of agent evaluation into semantic and behavioral dimensions with single-turn and multi-turn sub-dimensions
Identify the key metrics within each evaluation category, from coherence and faithfulness to tool selection and plan quality
Recognize the grounding symmetry: truthfulness for representations and goal achievement for behaviors

sections.title: Introduction and the Evaluation Map Overview
sections.summary: Ari Heluk introduces the presentation and divides agent evaluation into semantic (representations vs reality) and behavioral (actions/tools vs goal achievement) parts, each further split into single-turn and multi-turn aspects. A symmetry is noted: truthfulness grounds representations, while goal achievement grounds behaviors.

sections.title: Semantic Quality — Single Turn
sections.summary: Covers universal (non-agentic) virtues like consistency and safety for completeness, then value alignment, policy adherence, and RAG-specific evaluators: context recall correctness, comprehensiveness, faithfulness (distinct from answer-question relevance and from general factfulness). RAG evaluations examine relationships between pipeline parts.

sections.title: Semantic Quality — Multi-Turn
sections.summary: Addresses chat conversation history evaluation: consistency, topic adherence (sometimes allowing topic changes), and reasoning trace / Chain of Thought evaluation, described as groundbreaking progress in evaluating sequential multi-turn representational activities.

sections.title: Behavioral Quality — Single and Multi-Step
sections.summary: Single-step behavioral evaluation includes instruction following, tool characteristic extraction, tool selection, output quality, error handling, and format correctness. Multi-step evaluation examines whether actions converge toward goals and whether plans are consistent and high-quality. Both are grounded on external reality: representations on truthfulness, behaviors on goal achievement and utility.

sections.title: Practical Considerations
sections.summary: Lists cost and latency optimization, step count optimization, tracing and debugging, error management (tool usage errors vs semantic inference errors), offline vs online testing as distinct dimensions, and tool-specific metrics that can leverage traditional software testing for API-like tools.

sections.title: Eval Ops and Double-Tier Optimization
sections.summary: Introduces Eval Ops: when using LLM-as-judge, a single-tier approach only optimizes the agent, but a double-tier approach also optimizes the judge/evaluation flow for cost, latency, and uncertainty. Eval Ops is a special case of LLMOps operating on different entities, requiring different thinking, software, and resourcing.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.summary: Closing remarks encouraging viewers to consult source materials, acknowledge the presentation's likely obsolescence, and urging the community to make agents measurable, controllable, and aligned with human intentions.

limitations: The presentation only scratches the surface of practical considerations; several special cases and advanced topics are left uncovered due to time constraints.
The map does not fully incorporate offline vs online testing as dimensions, as including them would make the map more complicated.
The presenter acknowledges the presentation will likely be obsolete by the time it is released due to rapid developments in the field.
